UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                  BEFORE THE
                    FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Interconnection of Large Loads to the                  )       Docket No. RM26-4-000
Interstate Transmission System                         )



                  SUPPLEMENTAL COMMENTS OF ASHKAN YOUSEFI

I. Interest of the Commenter

       I submit these supplemental comments as an individual power systems engineer. I hold a
doctorate in electrical and computer engineering, I am a Chartered Professional Engineer
registered with Engineers Australia, and I am a Senior Member of the IEEE. I am resident in
Houston, Texas.

        My professional background bears directly on the questions raised in this proceeding. I
spent four years at Western Power, a transmission and distribution utility serving more than two
million customers, where my work included load flow, fault, contingency and reactive support
studies, and where I assessed and processed customer connection requests. I subsequently led
electricity market and dispatch simulation for a large industrial load at Ernst & Young's Power and
Utilities practice, and I held a postdoctoral fellowship at the University of California, Berkeley,
working on grid analytics and behind the meter storage. I currently lead an advisory practice that
performs site power viability and interconnection feasibility analysis for renewable developers,
asset managers and infrastructure investors, with active work in ERCOT and in the Australian
National Electricity Market.

       I note that the Commission's initial comment period in this docket closed in December
2025, and that the Commission has since issued show cause orders to the six jurisdictional regional
transmission organizations and independent system operators in Docket Nos. EL26-67-000
through EL26-72-000. The Commission stated that it would leave this docket open and encouraged
continued stakeholder participation. I offer these comments in that spirit, and I intend to address the
regional filings separately once they are submitted.

      I have no financial interest in the outcome of this proceeding beyond that of any practitioner
working in the field. I speak only for myself.

II. Summary of Recommendations



                                                  1
 The Commission has asked how large loads can be interconnected in a manner that is timely,
orderly, reliable and non-discriminatory. Much of the public discussion has treated this as a
question of process speed. I would suggest the more tractable problem is the quality of the
information the process runs on, and the assumptions embedded in the studies themselves. Faster
studies built on conservative deterministic inputs will produce faster overbuilding, at a cost that is
ultimately allocated to someone. My recommendations are as follows.

   1. The Commission should direct transmission providers to move from single point
       deterministic peak assumptions toward probabilistic large load study methods that state
       results as exceedance probabilities with explicit confidence intervals.

   2. Expedited study treatment for flexible loads should be conditioned on ex post verifiability of
       curtailment performance through telemetry and a defined measurement and verification
       standard, not on contractual attestation alone.

   3. Transmission providers should be required to publish hosting capacity, contingency margin
        and available headroom data in machine readable form, at a defined spatial and temporal
        granularity, so that prospective applicants can screen sites before entering a queue.

   4. Reliability evaluation of partial generator retirement to serve co-located load should be
       forward looking with respect to load growth in the affected area, and required network
       upgrades should be energized before the co-located load is served at full capacity.

   5. Where the Commission adopts a credit back mechanism for network upgrade costs, credits
       should be calibrated to realized coincident peak contribution rather than contracted or
       nameplate capacity.

III. Deterministic Peak Assumptions Overstate Required Network Reinforcement

        Large load interconnection studies inherit a methodology built for a different problem.
Conventional distribution and transmission planning practice evaluates a worst case coincident
peak, applies contingency criteria at that peak, and sizes reinforcement to the resulting deficit. This
is a sound approach when the load being studied is weather driven, highly coincident with system
peak, and poorly observable. It is a poor fit for large computing loads.

        Two properties of these loads matter. The first is that their load shape is comparatively flat,
with a high load factor and limited weather sensitivity. The second, which receives less attention, is
that their coincidence with system peak is genuinely uncertain rather than merely unknown.
Coincidence depends on the operator's workload scheduling, on cooling system behavior under
local ambient conditions, and increasingly on whether the operator is responding to price or



                                                  2
 curtailment signals. Treating that uncertainty as though it were a known worst case does not make
the study conservative in a useful sense. It makes the study insensitive to the single variable that
most affects the reinforcement conclusion.

        In my own work performing site viability analysis, the difference between a deterministic
worst case assumption and a probabilistic treatment of coincidence frequently changes the
reinforcement conclusion for a candidate site, and it does so in both directions. Some sites that
screen as infeasible under worst case assumptions are feasible with a modest and verifiable
curtailment obligation. Others that appear feasible on an average basis carry tail risk that a
deterministic study does not surface at all, because a single point estimate cannot express the shape
of a distribution. The planning question is not whether the load might coincide with peak. It is how
often, under what conditions, and with what consequence.

        I would therefore encourage the Commission to require that large load study reports
express results probabilistically. Concretely, a study should state the probability that the requested
load contributes to a binding constraint under specified contingency conditions, report that
probability with a confidence interval reflecting input uncertainty, and identify which input
assumptions the conclusion is most sensitive to. This is not a novel analytical demand.
Probabilistic resource adequacy assessment is already standard practice, and probabilistic
transmission planning methods are well developed in the literature and in several international
jurisdictions. What is missing is a requirement that large load studies use them, and a tariff
obligation to disclose the assumptions.

        A secondary benefit deserves mention. Deterministic studies are difficult for an applicant to
contest, because the disagreement reduces to competing assertions about a single number. A
probabilistic study with disclosed inputs and a sensitivity ranking gives both the transmission
provider and the applicant a shared basis for negotiating a flexibility obligation that avoids
reinforcement, which is precisely the outcome the Department of Energy's principles contemplate.

IV. Expedited Treatment for Flexible Load Requires Verifiable Performance

        The Commission has asked whether large loads and co-located facilities that agree to be
flexible and to curtail usage should move through studies more quickly, and whether such studies
might be completed within sixty days. In my view an expedited path for flexible load is justified
and technically achievable. It carries a specific failure mode that the tariff language should address
at the outset.




                                                  3
          If expedited treatment is granted on the strength of a contractual commitment to curtail, and
the reinforcement that would otherwise have been built is not built, then the reliability of the
resulting configuration depends entirely on performance of that commitment during precisely the
hours when the system is most stressed. A commitment that is not measured is not a commitment.
It is an assumption with a signature on it.

         The remedy is unglamorous and available. Curtailment performance should be verified
after the fact against a defined baseline, using interval telemetry at the point of interconnection at a
resolution no coarser than the market settlement interval. The tariff should specify the baseline
methodology, the notification lead time the load is obligated to honor, the tolerance band for
performance, and the consequence of non performance. That consequence should be graduated and
should escalate to reassessment of the load's study basis, because a load that persistently fails to
curtail is, in engineering terms, a firm load that has not been studied as one.

         There is precedent to draw on. Demand response measurement and verification protocols in
the organized markets already resolve most of the baseline questions, and utility interruptible
tariffs have long carried performance obligations with defined consequences. The Commission
need not invent a framework. It should require that one be specified before expedited treatment is
granted, rather than after the first stressed hour reveals that it was not.

       I would add a caution about the sixty day figure. A sixty day study is realistic for a site
where network data is current and the flexibility obligation is clearly defined, and unrealistic where
the study must first establish basic network conditions. This argues for the data availability
requirement discussed in the following section, since study duration is largely a function of how
much preparatory work each study must repeat.

V. Hosting Capacity and Contingency Margin Data Should Be Published in Machine
Readable Form

       A substantial share of interconnection queue congestion is caused by applications that
would never have been submitted had the applicant been able to assess the site beforehand. This is
not a controversial proposition among practitioners, but it is worth stating plainly because the
remedies usually proposed address the symptom. Deposit requirements, financial security and
readiness criteria filter speculative applications by making them expensive. Published data
prevents them by making them unnecessary.

     The scale of the problem is visible in the non jurisdictional market I work in most closely.
ERCOT has publicly reported a large load interconnection queue in the range of several hundred



                                                   4
 gigawatts, against a small fraction of that figure actually energized. ERCOT is not subject to the
Commission's jurisdiction and its connect and manage framework differs materially from the
jurisdictional regions, so I offer the comparison only as evidence of a general dynamic. When
applicants cannot screen sites, they apply everywhere plausible and let the study process do the
screening. The study process is the most expensive possible screening mechanism, and it is shared.

        Several utilities already publish hosting capacity maps, generally oriented toward
distributed generation on the distribution system. What large load applicants need is different in
scope and in granularity. I would suggest the Commission require transmission providers to
publish, at defined intervals and in a machine readable format rather than as static images or
portable document files, the available load headroom at each transmission substation or
interconnection point, the binding constraint associated with that headroom, the relevant
contingency margin, the study year and assumptions on which the figure rests, and the volume of
pending requests already allocated against it. That last element matters more than it might appear.
A site with headroom that has already been claimed by earlier queue positions is not available, and
an applicant who cannot see the pending allocation is being invited to file a request that cannot
succeed.

        Legitimate concerns exist about critical energy infrastructure information. Those concerns
are real and the Commission has an established framework for handling them. They do not justify
withholding aggregate headroom figures at substation level, which is information that any
competent consultant reconstructs from public planning documents at considerable cost and with
considerable error. The current arrangement does not protect the data. It taxes access to it and
distributes the results unevenly, which is difficult to reconcile with the non discrimination principle
this proceeding is meant to advance.

VI. Reliability Evaluation of Partial Retirement for Co-Located Load

       The Commission asked how reliability should be evaluated when an existing generator
seeks to partially shut down in order to serve a new large customer at the same site, including
whether future load growth should be considered and whether required upgrades must be
completed first. My view on both sub questions is affirmative, and for the same underlying reason.

        A partial retirement to serve co-located load changes the network twice. It removes
injection at a location where that injection was providing local voltage support and contributing to
contingency margin, and it adds withdrawal at the same location. The net effect on the surrounding
network is larger than either change considered alone, and it is not adequately captured by
comparing the site's net position before and after. The study must evaluate the post configuration


                                                  5
 against the same contingency criteria applied to any other material change, using the load forecast
that will actually obtain during the asset's life rather than the forecast that obtained when the
generator was originally interconnected.

        On the sequencing question, I would put the point more strongly than the ANOPR does.
Where the evaluation identifies network upgrades as necessary to maintain reliability in the post
configuration, serving the co-located load at full capacity before those upgrades are energized
means operating a knowingly deficient configuration for the duration of the construction period. If
the interim risk is judged acceptable, that judgment should be explicit, documented, and
accompanied by defined operating restrictions, rather than absorbed silently into the schedule. A
staged energization tied to upgrade milestones is a reasonable middle path and one that developers
can plan around.

VII. Cost Allocation and Credit Back Should Track Realized Coincident Peak

       On cost allocation, I support the principle that large loads should bear the cost of network
upgrades required for their interconnection, and I recognize the argument for crediting those costs
back over time as other users come to benefit from the reinforcement. The design question is what
quantity the credit is calibrated to.

        If credits are calibrated to contracted or nameplate capacity, the mechanism rewards the
applicant who requests the largest interconnection irrespective of what is ultimately used, and it
does so at the expense of users who paid for headroom that the requesting load never occupied.
Calibrating instead to realized coincident peak contribution, measured over a defined historical
window, aligns the credit with the burden the load actually places on the constrained element. It
also interacts constructively with the flexibility framework discussed above, since a load that
reliably curtails during constrained hours will show a lower coincident peak contribution and
should receive proportionally more favorable treatment. That is the correct incentive, and it is
created without any additional administrative apparatus.

VIII. Implementation and Pending Requests

         The Commission asked how to treat requests already under review when new requirements
take effect. I would suggest a transitional election rather than either a clean break or blanket
grandfathering. An applicant with a pending request should be permitted, within a defined window,
to elect treatment under the new framework without forfeiting queue position, on the condition that
any additional study required by the new framework is completed. Applicants who do not elect
should proceed under the rules in force when they applied.



                                                 6
          The data publication requirement discussed in Section V should not be subject to a
transition at all. It imposes no obligation on any applicant and it improves the information available
to every participant, including those in the existing queue. If anything it should be implemented
first, because several of the other reforms depend on it to function as intended.

IX. Conclusion

        The Commission is being asked to make an interconnection process faster while the volume
of requests entering it grows at a rate the process was never designed to absorb. Speed and
prudence are usually presented as a trade off in this debate. They are not entirely in tension. A large
share of the time consumed in these studies is spent reconstructing information that the
transmission provider already holds, and a large share of the cost is driven by conservatism that a
better characterization of uncertainty would remove. Publishing the data and modernizing the
study method address both problems at once, and they do so without asking the Commission to
choose between reliability and pace.

       I appreciate the opportunity to comment and would welcome the chance to provide further
technical detail if it would assist the Commission or its staff.



Respectfully submitted,


Ashkan (Ash) Yousefi, PhD
Chartered Professional Engineer, Engineers Australia
Senior Member, IEEE
Houston, Texas
ash@felixfusion.ai
